slides.heading: Public Health Nurse Bag Technique
slides.subtitle: A tool that lets the nurse perform procedures during a home visit with ease while preventing infection.

slides.heading: Principles of Bag Technique
bullets: Minimizes / prevents the spread of infection.
Saves time and effort in performing nursing procedures.
Should show effectiveness of total care given.
May be performed in various ways per agency policy/home situation — as long as infection transfer is always avoided.

slides.heading: Use of the Bag
bullets: Contains all articles/supplies/equipment for emergency needs.
Clean often; replace supplies; keep ready for use anytime.
Protect from contact with the patient's articles — the bag & contents are clean/sterile; the patient's articles are considered dirty/contaminated.
Arrange contents conveniently for efficiency.

slides.heading: Key Steps in Performing Bag Technique
bullets: Place the bag on a clean paper-lined table (clean side out, folded part touching the table).
Ask for water; take out towel & soap; wash hands.
Put on the apron (right side out); take out needed articles; close the bag and set aside.
Perform the nursing care; afterward clean items, wash hands, and return items.
Remove apron (soiled side in), fold lining into the bag, close it.
Record data and give instructions; make the next appointment.

slides.heading: Epidemiology — Definition
bullets: Study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states/events in populations, applied to prevention and control.
Distribution: analysis by time, place and person.
Determinants: biological, chemical, physical, social, cultural, economic, genetic and behavioral factors.

terms.definition: Observes distribution of disease/characteristics in populations.
Retrospective — proceeds backward from effect to cause.
Proceeds forward from cause to effect (prospective or retrospective).
A treatment/procedure is intentionally introduced and the result observed (e.g., randomized controlled trials).

slides.heading: Data Presentation
bullets: Line listing — organizes data during surveillance/outbreaks.
Histogram — frequency distribution of a continuous variable.
Scatter diagram — relationship between two continuous variables.
Bar chart, pie chart, population pyramid (count/% by age & sex), maps (geographic location).

slides.heading: PH Surveillance Systems (Philippines)
bullets: Notifiable Disease Reporting System (NDRS).
Field Health Service Information System (FHSIS).
National Epidemiology Sentinel Surveillance System (NESSS).
Expanded Program on Immunization Surveillance.
HIV/AIDS Registry.

slides.heading: Key Takeaways
bullets: Bag technique's overriding principle: prevent the transfer of infection.
Bag & contents = clean/sterile; patient's items = contaminated.
Epidemiology studies distribution (time/place/person) and determinants.
Case-control = backward (effect→cause); cohort = forward (cause→effect).
